title: Linear-sketch complexity of the nuclear norm
formal:
Determine the optimal number \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) of exact real linear measurements required to estimate the nuclear norm of an arbitrary real \(n\times n\) matrix with relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\), up to matching constant factors in \(n\), for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

The sketch is randomized and chosen independently of the input matrix. It must satisfy, for every fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\),
\[\Pr_\omega\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\le d_\omega(S_\omega A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\right]\ge\frac23,\]
where \(S_\omega:\mathbb R^{n\times n}\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(d_\omega\) is a decoder that receives only the sketch and the input-independent random choices. The quantity \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) is the smallest possible dimension \(m\).

Give an explicit asymptotic description \(g(n,\varepsilon)\) and prove that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) there exist \(0<c_\varepsilon\le C_\varepsilon<\infty\) and \(N_\varepsilon\) such that
\[c_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge N_\varepsilon).\]
The constants may depend on the fixed accuracy, but not on \(n\). Logarithmic factors in \(n\) must be resolved; determining only a polynomial exponent does not meet this target.
why: Determining this complexity would explain whether summing singular values permits a materially smaller linear summary than storing a general matrix, and exactly how much compression is possible. It would also locate a central matrix norm within the sharply differing sketching behavior of the Schatten family.
status_note: The exact asymptotic order up to constant factors remains source-open in the checked material. The original question is Woodruff’s 2014 survey Open Question 4. The 2019 journal article’s model and linear lower bound were checked. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found Yang’s arXiv:2608.22247v3, revised 27 August 2026: its stated near-quadratic lower and upper bounds leave logarithmic factors unresolved, as explicitly discussed in §6. This review inspected its model, theorem statement and remaining-gap discussion, not a full independent verification of its 94-page proof; no verified journal acceptance is asserted. The recent bounds are therefore identified as preprint claims, and even as stated they do not complete this card’s matching-constant-factor criterion.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Open Question 4 asks for the optimal constant-factor nuclear-norm sketch dimension; at that time the survey reports a substantial gap below the trivial \(O(n^2)\) storage bound.

The published general-sketch lower bound reaches \(\Omega(n)\) for sufficiently accurate constant-factor nuclear-norm estimation. The same paper distinguishes this statement from bilinear-sketch and finite-bit streaming results.

Preprint v3 of Yang claims bounds within polylogarithmic factors of \(n^2\), together with an upper bound saving a logarithmic factor up to iterated logarithms. It explicitly leaves the optimal logarithmic dependence unresolved. The result is recorded as a recent unverified theorem claim, not a completed resolution of this target.

importance.reason: A long-standing quantitative question about a standard matrix norm in the general sketching model. Its importance comes from the gap between neighboring norms, applications of compact matrix summaries, and the need to distinguish arbitrary linear measurements from restricted sketches and bit-space bounds.

sentences: The nuclear norm of a matrix is the sum of its singular values.
The question asks for the smallest number of randomized exact real linear measurements that suffice to approximate this norm for every fixed input matrix.
The requested answer must give matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors for each fixed relative accuracy.
Published results separate this matrix problem from ordinary vector norms, bilinear sketches and finite-bit streaming complexity.
An August 2026 preprint claims near-quadratic bounds but leaves logarithmic factors unresolved, and its proof is not independently verified by this review.

definitions:
Let \(n\) be any positive integer. For a real square matrix \(A\), its singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_n(A)\) are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\), with multiplicities and zeros included. Its nuclear norm, also called the trace norm or Schatten-1 norm, is
\[\|A\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i(A).\]
No symmetry, positive-semidefiniteness, rank, sparsity, integrality or bounded-entry promise is imposed. In particular, this is not the entrywise sum of absolute values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues, and for that restricted class the nuclear norm equals the trace; the target covers all real matrices.

An \(m\)-measurement randomized linear sketch for given \(n,\varepsilon\) is specified by an input-independent probability space of random seeds \(\omega\), a real linear map \(S_\omega\), and a decoding function \(d_\omega:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\). Equivalently, each measurement has the form
\[(S_\omega A)_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n B_{tij}(\omega)A_{ij},\qquad1\le t\le m,\]
where all coefficients are fixed once the seed is sampled, before inspecting any entry of \(A\). The map may depend on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(A\). The seed may also specify independent decoder randomness. The coefficient functions and the combined decoding map \((\omega,y)\mapsto d_\omega(y)\) are measurable with respect to their probability space and the usual Borel sigma-algebra on finite-dimensional real spaces, so every displayed success probability is defined.

All randomness is over the seed. The matrix is fixed before that seed is chosen, with the quantifier order \(\exists\text{ sketch distribution}\;\forall A\;\Pr_\omega[\text{success on }A]\ge2/3\). The same seed need not work simultaneously for all matrices. Conversely, a guarantee only for a random input matrix is insufficient. For \(A=0\), success requires the output to be exactly zero. For nonzero inputs the error bound is multiplicative, equivalently \(|d_\omega(S_\omega A)-\|A\|_*|\le\varepsilon\|A\|_*\).

The cost is the fixed number \(m\) of data-dependent real scalars retained. Coefficients, measurements and arithmetic are exact real objects. Their bit lengths, the description of the seed, evaluation time, and the decoder's auxiliary working space are not counted. No finite-precision or efficient-sampling requirement is added. The decoder can be nonlinear and have unbounded computational cost. This is an information measure for general linear sketches, not a claim of a Turing-machine implementation. Separate choices of distribution and decoder for each \(n,\varepsilon\) are allowed; an algorithm constructing them uniformly in polynomial time is not part of the target.

Define
\[m_\varepsilon(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{ an admissible }m\text{-measurement sketch satisfies the stated guarantee}\}.\]
This minimum is finite and attained as a minimum over integers: retaining all \(n^2\) entries is a linear sketch from which the norm is defined exactly. The target seeks a noncircular asymptotic description of this optimization, with upper bounds witnessed by admissible sketch distributions and lower bounds applying to every such distribution and decoder.

A restricted bilinear sketch retains a matrix \(UAV\) for input-independent matrices \(U\) and \(V\); its scalar entry count is one possible general linear-sketch dimension. General sketches are not restricted to this form. Lower bounds for one selected architecture do not automatically extend to all real linear maps. Likewise, bits of streaming memory and real measurement dimension are different resources. An entry update can be reflected linearly in the sketch, but this does not identify the number of exact counters with their finite binary storage cost.

The source asks for a constant-factor approximation without fixing the constant. This review spells out the family of fixed relative accuracies \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with constant success probability \(2/3\), in the standard model made explicit in the subsequent literature. Each accuracy is held constant while \(n\to\infty\); the answer need not optimize a joint regime where \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\). The requested precision for the optimal dimension is equality of asymptotic order up to multiplicative constants, including every unbounded logarithmic factor.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular asymptotic description of \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with the quantifiers and input domain above. An upper bound must give a valid input-independent sketch and decoder with the per-matrix success guarantee. A lower bound must apply to arbitrary measurable decoders and all general randomized real linear maps. Bounds matching only up to polylogarithmic factors, only the exponent in \(n^{\alpha+o(1)}\), a result confined to positive semidefinite matrices, or a finite-bit streaming bound alone do not determine the requested order. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the sketch's relative error; the benchmark's default additive numerical tolerance does not replace the required asymptotic precision.

source_formulation.text: Woodruff asks for the optimal dimension of a linear sketch that approximates the Schatten-1, or nuclear, norm within a constant factor. The question contrasts it with the much better understood Frobenius and spectral norms.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Question 4, with the general real linear-sketch model and constant-factor precision made explicit below

context_blocks.text: The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.
